newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian police chief warns of war danger.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian police chief warns of war danger.

text.p: A Bosnian police chief has warned NATO that a continuing spate of ethnic bomb attacks could erupt into "real armed conflict" in Bosnia.
"There were two explosions last night in the Moslem village of Potocani, northwest of Mahala in eastern Bosnia," U.N. International Police Task Force spokesman Andrea Angelli told Reuters.
Two houses were damaged but there were no injuries, he said.
The incidents occured hours after Zvornik police chief Colonel Dragomir Vasic warned the situation in the Serb-held area of the three villages recently resettled by Moslem refugees was very tense.
"An incident could break out at any moment which could grow into a real armed conflict," Bosnian Serb news agency SRNA quoted him as saying in letters to local NATO commanders.
Angelli also reported serious harassment of Moslems in Serb town of Teslic.
In four separate incidents on Monday several persons entered Moslem houses, threatened the occupants and opened fire on their houses, he said.
"The IPTF is very concerned about it," he said.
U.S. peace envoy John Kornblum also conveyed his concerns to the Bosnian presidency Serb member Momcilo Krajisnik over the destruction.

"Kornblum said he was worried over houses that were destroyed on the inter-entity boundary line," Krajisnik said after meeting Mike Parmley, the U.S. charge d'affaires in Sarajevo, who conveyed Kornblum's message.
The tensions were rising in Bosnia despite an attempt by NATO commanders to try to halt a spate of bombing and arson attacks apparently aimed at preventing refugees from returning to their homes.
NATO condemned the destruction of scores of homes in northwest Bosnia last week, saying the incidents appeared to be well-orchestrated attacks.
More than 90 Moslem houses and two mosques were destroyed in several abandoned villages near Serb-held Prijedor in the course of several hours last week.
NATO said the demolition around Prijedor appeared systematic. Several 10 kg (20 pound) anti-tank mines were rigged to each house.
In Croat-held Drvar to the south, 65 Serb houses in two villages were torched over several days.
Under a U.S.-brokered peace accord signed last December, Moslem, Croat and Serb leaders agreed to guarantee refugees the right to return to their homes.
But during 10 months of peace only a small number of people have dared to cross back to territory controlled by another ethnic group.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees has been struggling to rebuild trust between divided communities and NATO has stepped up patrols to try to combat the destruction of houses in sensitive areas and catch bombers.
